frase_gancho.texto: Diego Rivera built this pyramid to display pieces from his collection outdoors.

puente_narrativo.texto: Cross the garden to the exhibition hall at the far end, where part of Frida’s wardrobe is on display.

guion_corto.texto: In the middle of the garden stands a red pyramid that is not an ancient ruin. Diego Rivera had it built, and it was constructed in the twentieth century. It served to hold valuable pieces from his collection. Diego gathered more than sixty thousand pre-Hispanic objects, and he wanted to show them as something alive, not as antiquities behind glass. That is why the pieces are outdoors, among the plants. He began building the Anahuacalli Museum, made of volcanic stone, in nineteen forty-two. This pyramid is a small version of that idea. Take a moment to look at its steps. Notice how it looks against the blue wall.

guion_largo.texto:
This pyramid looks ancient, but it was built in the twentieth century. Diego Rivera had it made in the twentieth century, inside the Casa Azul. It is painted red, with a yellow central staircase, and on its steps and in its niches pieces from his collection of pre-Hispanic art were placed.

Diego was a tireless collector. It is said that he gathered more than sixty thousand pre-Hispanic pieces over the course of his life. He bought many of them with the money he earned from his murals. He did not think of them as luxury objects. For him, they were works of art by the ancient peoples, and he wanted them to be seen.

Behind that collection lies a simple idea. The peoples of ancient Mexico made art of enormous quality. Diego wanted it to be seen as art. That is why he placed the pieces in a garden, outdoors, among plants, as they once stood in the ancient ceremonial centers.

That idea grew over time. In nineteen forty-two, Diego began the construction of the Anahuacalli Museum, a building made of volcanic stone on a lava field left by the Xitle volcano. It blends modern art with pre-Hispanic aesthetics and holds around thirty-nine thousand pre-Hispanic pieces, of which about two thousand are on display. The pyramid in the garden of the Casa Azul can be seen as a small trial run of that same idea.

There is a question worth asking when you look at the pyramid. What changes when an ancient piece is placed outdoors, among the plants, and not behind glass? Perhaps it loses protection, but it gains context.

The word Anahuacalli is usually translated as house of the Anáhuac, which was the name given to the Valley of Mexico. Diego wanted a building that would resemble a modern pyramid, and he made it with the same volcanic stone found in the region. The pyramid in the garden of the Casa Azul served as a trial run, because there he had already thought about how to place the pieces and how to blend them with the landscape.

The Anahuacalli Museum is part of the same trust that looks after the Casa Azul, the Diego Rivera and Frida Kahlo Museums Trust. That is why the pyramid in the garden can be seen as part of a shared story, that of pre-Hispanic art and the way Diego understood it.

The pieces on display may vary over time. You will not always see the same figures on the steps. What does not change is the idea. It is a pyramid made by a twentieth-century painter to honor the art of the ancient peoples.

texto: Notice the colors of the pyramid: red, with a yellow staircase
Look for the pre-Hispanic pieces placed on the steps and in the niches
Imagine how those pieces change when they are among plants, in the sun and in the rain

texto.Structure: stepped pyramid built by Diego Rivera in the 20th century
texto.Function: to display pieces from his pre-Hispanic collection outdoors
texto.Diego’s Collection: more than 60,000 pre-Hispanic pieces, according to the museum

texto.pregunta: Myth: The pyramid in the garden is an authentic pre-Hispanic ruin that appeared when the house was built.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It is a modern construction, made by Diego Rivera in the twentieth century. The pieces displayed on it are indeed pre-Hispanic.
